title: How Can a Bridge Hold Up So Much Weight?
question: How can a bridge hold up so much weight?
answer: Bridges use clever shapes. Arches, triangles and cables turn heavy weight into squeezing and pulling, and pass it safely down into the strong ground.

visual.what: Huy, Hùng, Bối and Beo stand on a riverbank watching a big loaded truck drive across a long bridge. Beo hugs Hùng's leg and peeks out.

parts.text: Huy, look at that truck! It is heavier than an elephant. Why doesn't the bridge just snap?
Will it fall in the water?
No, Beo, it is safe. Great question, Bối. And here is a surprise. In Greece there is a stone bridge about 3,300 years old, and people still use it today.

visual.what: Huy talks to camera. Behind him Hùng carries a wobbly box full of rulers, sticks, paper and toy blocks.

parts.text: Today we will find out how a bridge can hold up so much weight. We will meet squeezing, pulling, a clever curve, and a shape that refuses to squash.
And I brought lots of things to test!

visual.what: Bối flexes her arm like a strongwoman next to a drawing of a steel beam and a giant rock. Beo holds up a huge bottle of glue.

parts.text: Easy! Bridges are made of super strong stuff. Thick steel and giant rocks!
Or glue! Lots and lots of glue!

visual.what: Side by side, a pile of rocks lying in a river with no way across, and a tall steel bridge over the river.

parts.text: Glue would be very sticky, Beo. Bối, that is a smart guess. Strong materials really do matter, and most big bridges today are made mostly of steel. But a pile of rocks is not a bridge.

visual.what: Hùng holds one stick of dry spaghetti that has just snapped in two, pieces flying. Next to him is a small, strong spaghetti bridge made of triangles.

parts.text: Snap! Oops, there goes dinner.
One stick of spaghetti snaps easily. Yet students build bridges out of spaghetti that are surprisingly strong. So the secret is not just what a bridge is made of. It is also the shape.

visual.what: A simple bridge with a car on it. Big arrows show the car's weight pushing down, going through the bridge and into the ground at both ends.

parts.text: Everything on Earth is pulled down by gravity. That pull is what we feel as weight. A bridge has one big job. Catch that weight and pass it along into the strong ground.

visual.what: Hùng lays a ruler across two stacks of books on a table. Bối gets ready to press the middle with one finger.

parts.text: Let's build the simplest bridge, a beam bridge. A beam is just a long, flat piece, like a plank across a stream.
One ruler bridge, ready. Your turn, Bối.

visual.what: Close view of the ruler bending down in the middle under Bối's finger, the ends still resting on the books.

parts.text: When I press the middle, it bends!
Yes. The middle is farthest from the supports, so that is where a beam bends the most.

visual.what: Zoom into the bent ruler. Little arrows on the top edge point inward, labelled squeezed. Little arrows on the bottom edge point outward, labelled stretched.

parts.text: Now look closely. When a beam bends, its top gets squeezed together, and its bottom gets stretched apart.
The ruler does two jobs?
Yes, Beo. One ruler, two jobs at once.

visual.what: Huy holds up a card with a bridge and a down arrow going into the ground.

parts.text: Takeaway one. A bridge must pass weight into the ground, and that squeezes or stretches its parts.

visual.what: Two drawings. A sponge being pressed by two hands, labelled compression, squeezing. A rubber band being pulled by two hands, labelled tension, pulling.

parts.text: Engineers, the people who design bridges, have special words for this. Squeezing is called compression. Pulling and stretching is called tension.

visual.what: Bối squishes her hands together then pulls them apart. Beo copies her, squishing his own cheeks.

parts.text: Compression, squish! Tension, stretch!
Squish! Squish!
Perfect. You both sound like engineers already.

visual.what: A stone block with hands pressing it, a green tick. The same stone being pulled apart with a crack, a red cross. A steel bar with two green ticks.

parts.text: Here is the important part. Stone and brick are very strong when you squeeze them. But pull on them and they crack quite easily. Steel copes well with both.

visual.what: Bối looks worried in front of an old stone bridge covered in moss. Huy points to it with a smile.

parts.text: So stone is bad for bridges?
Not at all! Some stone bridges have lasted thousands of years. Builders just had to find a shape that squeezes the stone and pulls it as little as possible.

visual.what: Huy holds a sponge in one hand and a rubber band in the other.

parts.text: Takeaway two. Every part of a bridge is squeezed or pulled, so builders pick the right material and the right shape for each job.

visual.what: A stone arch bridge with a weight on top. Arrows follow the curve around and down both sides into the ground.

parts.text: That shape is the arch. When weight presses on the top of an arch, the curve passes it around and down both sides into the ground.

visual.what: An arch made of wedge shaped stones, one stone pulled out beside it and labelled wedge, next to a slice of cake of the same shape. Small arrows show each stone pressing on its neighbours.

parts.text: An arch is built from wedge shaped stones. A wedge is wide at one end and narrow at the other, like a slice of cake. Each stone presses on its neighbours, so every stone is squeezed. Just what stone likes.
Cake? Can I have a slice?

visual.what: Hùng has built a small arch from soft toy foam blocks on the table. He has just lifted out the top block, and the other blocks tumble down onto the table around him.

parts.text: The stone at the very top is called the keystone. It locks all the others in place, like the last piece of a puzzle.
I took out the top block, and the whole arch fell down! Oops.

visual.what: An arch with arrows pushing outward at its two feet, and big strong blocks at each end labelled abutment pushing back. A small inset shows Bối standing with her legs wide.

parts.text: An arch also pushes outward at its feet, like your feet trying to slide apart when you stand with your legs wide. So builders put strong blocks at each end, called abutments, to push back and hold the arch together.

visual.what: A heavy wooden cart rolling on an old stone arch bridge. A layer of broken stones above the arch is labelled rubble, and the arch stones have small arrows pressing tighter together.

parts.text: So if a heavy cart rolls on top, the stones squeeze together even tighter?
Exactly! In old stone arches, more weight made the stones press together harder. Builders even piled rubble, which means broken stones, on top to make the bridge heavier and steadier.

visual.what: A timeline from about 2,000 years ago to today. At the start, Roman builders in tunics stack stones. At the end, a modern car drives over the same old stone arch bridge.

parts.text: That is why arches last. About 2,000 years ago the Romans built hundreds of stone arch bridges, and many are still standing. Some even carry cars today.

visual.what: Huy stands under a big drawn stone arch, arms out like the arch.

parts.text: Takeaway three. An arch turns weight into squeezing and sends it down into strong ground at its ends.

visual.what: Hùng holds up a square and a triangle made of craft sticks joined with loose pins at the corners.

parts.text: Now meet a shape that refuses to squash.
Here is a square and a triangle made of sticks. The pins at the corners are loose. Give them a push, Bối.

visual.what: Left, the stick square flopped into a leaning diamond shape. Right, the stick triangle staying perfectly in shape while Bối pushes it.

parts.text: The square flopped into a diamond! But the triangle won't budge!
A triangle cannot change shape unless one of its sides gets longer or shorter. That makes it super stiff.

visual.what: A truss bridge made of steel triangles. Some pieces are coloured blue and labelled squeezed, others red and labelled pulled.

parts.text: A bridge made of triangles is called a truss bridge. Each straight piece is mostly just squeezed or just pulled, not bent. And that is much easier for thin pieces than bending. A thin piece can pull well, and when pieces are joined in triangles, they hold each other in place.

visual.what: The spaghetti truss bridge from earlier holding a small toy car. Beo stares at it with wide eyes.

parts.text: That is the spaghetti secret. One stick snaps when you bend it. But joined in triangles, lots of weak sticks become one strong bridge. Trusses use material well, so they cost less to build too.
Strong spaghetti!

visual.what: Five small bridge drawings in a row, labelled beam, cantilever, arch, suspension and cable stayed. The suspension and cable stayed bridges show steel cables holding the road.

parts.text: Engineers mix these ideas. There are five main kinds of bridge. Beam, cantilever, arch, suspension, and cable stayed. A cantilever is an arm that sticks out, held at only one end. Suspension and cable stayed bridges hang the road from steel cables, which are great at being pulled.

visual.what: Four boxes in a row with arrows between them, labelled research, design, test, build. In the test box, a small model bridge sits in front of a fan blowing wind.

parts.text: Before a big bridge is built, engineers research, design and test their ideas, often with models. They make sure it can stand up to heavy loads, strong wind, and even earthquakes.

visual.what: Huy holds up the stiff stick triangle and smiles.

parts.text: Takeaway four. Triangles keep their shape, so a truss turns many thin pieces into one strong bridge.

visual.what: A flat sheet of paper laid across two stacks of books. Hùng places one coin in the middle and the paper sags down to the table.

parts.text: Here is a check you can try at home. Lay a sheet of paper across two stacks of books, and put a coin in the middle.
One coin, coming up.
It flopped right down.

visual.what: The same paper folded back and forth like a fan, laid across the books, holding a small stack of coins. Beo points at the coins counting on his fingers.

parts.text: Now fold the same paper back and forth, like a paper fan, and lay it across again.
It holds lots of coins! The folds make little triangles!
One, two, three, lots!

visual.what: Hùng slides a second sheet of paper, bent into a curve, under a flat sheet, with the curve's ends pushed against the two book stacks. Coins sit on top.

parts.text: Or bend a second sheet into a curve under the flat one, with its ends pushed against the books.
Now you have an arch, and the books are your abutments.
Same paper, new shape, much stronger!

visual.what: An arch, a truss triangle and a cable bridge side by side, each with arrows sending weight down into the ground.

parts.text: So how does a bridge hold so much weight? With clever shapes. Arches, triangles and cables turn heavy weight into squeezing and pulling, and pass it safely into the ground.

visual.what: The old stone Zhaozhou Bridge in China with one big flat arch and small open arches in its sides, river water flowing through them. Beo points and grins.

parts.text: Fun fact. The Zhaozhou Bridge in China was built of stone about 1,400 years ago, and it still stands. Little extra arches in its sides let floodwater rush through.
A bridge with windows!

visual.what: All four look up at a big plane flying over the bridge. A red subscribe button with the words Ask Huy floats in the corner.

parts.text: Huy, if bridges need the ground, how does a giant plane stay up with nothing under it?
Ooh, that is next time's question! Subscribe to Ask Huy so you don't miss it. Bye, bridge builders!
Bye!
Bye bye!

facts.claim: Possibly the oldest surviving arch bridge, the Arkadiko Bridge in Greece, dates to about 1300 BC (about 3,300 years ago) and local people still use it.
In recent centuries large bridges are made mostly of steel.
Model bridges made of spaghetti show that a truss can make a strong structure from weak pieces; spaghetti breaks easily if bent.
Bridges carry weight (loads) caused by gravity and pass it into the ground; structures are designed to withstand gravity loads.
Beam bridges are one of the five major types of bridge.
A bending beam is squeezed on top and stretched on the bottom, and bends most in the middle between supports.
facts.source: Basic school science (supported by Truss bridge: lower members in tension and bending, top members in compression)

facts.claim: Members of a structure act in tension (pulling) or compression (squeezing).
Stone and brick are strong in compression but cannot resist much force in tension.
Steel copes well with both squeezing and pulling.
facts.source: Basic school knowledge (supported by Truss bridge: iron rods used for tension members)

facts.claim: Some stone bridges have lasted thousands of years.
Masonry arch bridges are designed to be kept under constant compression.
Arches pass weight down to their supports and push outward (horizontal thrust), which is held by abutments at each end.
Roman arches used wedge-shaped stones (voussoirs); a keystone at the top bore the weight of the rest.
In early compression arch bridges, the more weight put on the bridge, the stronger it became; fill such as compacted rubble was added above the arch to increase dead weight.
The Romans built hundreds of stone bridges (330 listed by O'Connor), many still standing and some still carrying vehicles.
A truss bridge is made of connected elements usually forming triangles, whose members act mainly in tension or compression.
A triangle cannot change shape unless a side changes length, so it is stiff.
facts.source: Basic school knowledge (supported by Truss bridge)

facts.claim: Truss bridges are economical because they use materials efficiently.
There are five major types of bridges: beam, cantilever, arch, suspension and cable-stayed.
In a suspension bridge the cables are in tension.
Major structural projects go through research, design, testing and construction, and structures are designed to withstand gravity and wind loads and natural disasters.
The Zhaozhou Bridge in China (605 CE, about 1,400 years ago) is the oldest surviving arch bridge in China, wholly stone, with open spandrel arches allowing greater passage for floodwaters.

description: Why doesn't a bridge snap when a heavy truck drives over it? Huy, Hùng, Bối and little Beo find out how squeezing, pulling, arches and triangles help bridges carry huge weights, with a safe paper-and-coins test kids can try at home. A calm, accurate science explainer for children aged 6 to 12 and the grown-ups watching with them.

cast.name: Huy
cast.role: the host (25): curious, warm, a little funny; explains

cast.name: Hùng
cast.role: Huy's younger brother (21), his hands-on assistant: sets up and runs the experiments and demos, brings things, now and then a funny little mishap

cast.name: Bối
cast.role: an 8-year-old girl who asks, guesses and tries things

cast.name: Beo
cast.role: Bối's 5-year-old little brother: curious, makes funny innocent guesses
